title: Index vs full scan: count the rows you touch
prompt:
You're building a tiny in-memory table for the reading app's reading_sessions. The starter already does full scans: to answer any query it reads every row. Your job is to add indexes so that equality and range lookups read only the rows they need, and to report how much work each query did, like a mini EXPLAIN.

Implement class Table:

  • new Table(rows) and insert(row) store rows in insertion order (the "heap").
  • createIndex(column) builds an index on that column: a list of [value, rowPosition] pairs sorted by value (then by position). It must stay correct after later inserts.
  • findRange(column, lo, hi) returns rows with lo <= row[column] <= hi, and findEqual(column, v) is findRange(column, v, v). Both return { rows, plan, touched, comparisons }:
    • rows: matches ordered by the column value, then insertion order.
    • plan: 'index' if the column has an index, otherwise 'scan'.
    • touched: how many rows were read from the heap. A scan reads all of them; an index lookup reads only the matches.
    • comparisons: how many index entries you compared during binary search (for a scan, use the number of rows).
const t = new Table(sessions);          // 1,000 rows
t.findEqual('classId', 'c7');           // { plan: 'scan',  touched: 1000, rows: [20 rows] }
t.createIndex('classId');
t.findEqual('classId', 'c7');           // { plan: 'index', touched: 20,   comparisons: ~20 }

tests.name: without an index: a full scan touches every row
with an index: same rows, but only the matches are touched
binary search: ~log2(n) comparisons, even at 100,000 rows
range query on an indexed number column
the index stays correct after inserts
no match: empty result, nothing touched
an index on one column doesn't help queries on another

hints: An index is just a second copy of one column, kept sorted, with a pointer back to the row: [[value, position], ...]. Build it with this.rows.map((r, pos) => [r[column], pos]) and sort by value, then position.

To find the rows between lo and hi, you need two positions in the sorted index: the first entry >= lo and the first entry > hi. Everything between them matches. Find each with a binary search, counting one comparison per loop iteration. Only then look up the actual rows by position (that's touched).

The binary search shape:

lowerBound(idx, v, count) {
  let lo = 0, hi = idx.length;
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    count.n++;
    if (idx[mid][0] < v) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;
  }
  return lo;
}

upperBound is identical with <=. In insert, use upperBound to find where the new [value, pos] goes and splice it in.
explain:
A real database index is a B-tree: the same idea as your sorted array, but split into pages of a few hundred keys each, so finding one key among 100 million rows takes about 4 page reads instead of a 27-step binary search over one giant array, and inserts don't shift everything. Your touched is what Postgres calls rows read from the heap, and EXPLAIN shows the same choice you made: Seq Scan versus Index Scan.

Notice the cost you paid: every insert now also updates every index. That's the real trade-off. Indexes make reads on that column fast and make every write a bit slower and the table bigger.

Say it: "The teacher dashboard filters sessions by class_id, so I'd add an index on (class_id, created_at). That turns a scan of 50 million rows into reading the 30 that match. I wouldn't index every column, because each index slows down writes, and our write path is hot at 8am."
